extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, damages experts, and legal scholars drafting or applying jury instructions for patent reasonable-royalty damages (U.S. courts)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and evaluative standards for determining reasonable royalty patent damages in U.S. litigation, including a proposed four-factor framework, guidance on FRAND/SEP contexts, apportionment, and calculation methods (lump sum vs. running royalties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent damages policy objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: An accurate assessment of damages should award the patent holder the market value of a license — the amount on which a willing licensor and a willing licensee would have agreed in an arm's-length transaction before the infringer committed to using the patented technology (ex ante).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages should most closely restore the parties to their ex ante positions; should neither under-incentivize invention nor overcompensate patentees so as to impede innovation. The assessment should focus on the incremental value of the patented technology for the intended use compared to the best available alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ex ante hypothetical negotiation as the baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical negotiation date should be ex ante — before the alleged infringer invested in, or a standard-setting organization committed to, the allegedly infringing technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factfinder should evaluate what a willing licensor and willing licensee would have agreed to pre-investment (pre-standard). This baseline precludes valuing the patent based on post-investment lock-in or other ex post events, which can inflate royalty rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude ex post considerations (lock-in costs and related premiums)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let ex post events (investments made after the hypothetical date, lock-in costs, litigation-threat premiums, etc.) 'pollute' the ex ante hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should prevent consideration of the alleged infringer's lock-in costs or settlement-induced premiums when estimating the royalty the parties would have agreed to ex ante. Evidence and licenses reflecting ex post bargaining must be scrutinized for such taint (see 'book of wisdom' caution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment — award only incremental value attributable to the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Any royalty award must be apportioned to reflect no more than the incremental value that is contributed by the patent(s)-in-suit, distinguished from the value of non-patented elements, manufacturing, business risks, or improvements added by the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the smallest saleable patent-practicing unit when appropriate; separate and quantify the portion of value attributable to the patented feature(s) versus other features. Factor and jury instructions must emphasize apportionment as central to accurate damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Georgia-Pacific factors as an evaluative framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifteen Georgia-Pacific factors are an unprioritized, overlapping laundry list that are out of date and provide insufficient guidance on weighting and balancing for juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgia-Pacific should not be treated as a talisman. Courts should not mechanically list or require all fifteen factors; instead adopt a concise, coherent set of instructions that direct juries to the economically-relevant considerations (see proposed replacement framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor One: The incremental value contributed by the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the incremental value that the claimed invention contributed to the accused product (i.e., the value over and above the best available alternative at the hypothetical negotiation date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the factfinder on the incremental contribution of the patented feature to the product's value; exclude value that would have existed absent the patented feature or that is attributable to conventional elements or alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Two: The value contributed by factors other than the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and quantify value in the accused product that is attributable to non-claimed features, complementary technologies, business practices, or other sources not claimed by the patent(s)-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor supports apportionment: the jury should reduce any award to exclude value from non-patented elements or separate contributions from other technologies or patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Three: Comparable agreements (licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prior licenses and comparable agreements as evidence of a reasonable royalty only where they are sufficiently comparable and not tainted by ex post bargaining or coercive litigation dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and juries must ask whether a prior license is actually comparable to the hypothetical negotiation at issue (timing, scope, parties, threats of injunction, etc.). Settlement agreements and licenses obtained under the explicit or implicit threat of prohibitive orders are suspect and may be unreliable indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Four: Commercial considerations showing desire or reluctance to license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective commercial evidence that would show whether the parties would have been inclined to license (or reluctant to) at the hypothetical negotiation date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence might include product profitability, market demand for the patented capability, competitive relationships, and the licensor/licensee commercial context; such evidence must be tied to ex ante expectations and apportioned to the patented contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions regarding FRAND/SEP contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is essential to a standard and subject to a FRAND commitment, the reasonable royalty must reflect only the contribution of the patented technology to the standard's capabilities and must exclude value attributable to the standard as a whole or to other patents incorporated in the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries must apportion awards to exclude value attributable to the ability to practice the standard itself and to other patents. Where applicable (e.g., IEEE commitments), courts should instruct juries on specific FRAND-language considerations (contribution of claimed invention to smallest saleable product, comparable licenses not obtained under threat, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty stacking (aggregate royalties) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: If, at the time of the hypothetical negotiation, parties would have expected that many patents must be licensed to practice the product or standard, the aggregate royalties (royalty stack) are a relevant factor in what a licensor/licensee would agree to pay or accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parties in a pre-standard or pre-investment negotiation would consider aggregate royalties required to practice the standard or to produce the accused product; juries should consider this to avoid an award that, in aggregate with other royalties, would be excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type[s] of reasonable royalties — lump sum versus running royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalties can take several forms (one-time lump-sum payments or running royalties), and the jury should be instructed to decide which form is appropriate based on evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define lump sum and running royalties clearly for the jury. If running royalties are used, instruct juries on how to compute them (identify base, apportion the base, determine royalty rate, total damages = apportioned base × royalty rate). The instruction should reflect the parties' likely bargaining form at the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to calculate running royalty damages
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate a running royalty: identify total sales revenue of the smallest saleable component practicing the invention; identify the apportioned base (portion attributable to the claimed invention); determine the royalty rate the parties would have agreed to; multiply apportioned base by royalty rate to get total damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jurors with concrete steps and party contentions for each step (e.g., disputed base amount or rate). Emphasize apportionment in identifying the base and require factual support for claimed bases and rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest saleable patent-practicing unit principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicable, royalties should be based on the smallest saleable patent-practicing unit rather than the entire multi-component product, unless facts support a different approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle aids apportionment: where the SSU is multi-component, the patentee must further separate value attributable to the patented feature. Courts should instruct juries that SSU is typically the appropriate revenue base for royalty calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony: admissibility and gatekeeping (methodology must assess ex ante royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert opinions regarding reasonable royalties must be grounded in ex ante facts or expectations and use methodologies reasonably calculated to assess the royalty that would have been agreed to in the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (as gatekeepers) should exclude methodologies that are not reasonably calculated to approximate the ex ante hypothetical negotiation; expert testimony relying on post hoc or tainted evidence should be excluded or given appropriate limiting instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare and weigh Georgia-Pacific factors only insofar as they illuminate ex ante expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: If any Georgia-Pacific factors are considered, they should be used only to the extent they illuminate ex ante expectations relevant to the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix guidance maps each Georgia-Pacific factor's relevance to an ex ante analysis (e.g., Factor 6 relevant only to the extent it illuminates ex ante expectations about convoyed sales). Courts should explicitly explain which Georgia-Pacific factors matter and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude or discount licenses/settlements obtained under coercive litigation pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses or settlements arising from litigation and obtained under the threat of prohibitive orders are poor proxies for voluntary ex ante agreements and must be scrutinized or excluded as comparable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Federal Circuit authority (e.g., LaserDynamics, Lucent, Uniloc) recognizing settlements/licences tainted by coercion may be unsuitable to prove reasonable royalty. Consider context, timing, and comparability before admitting or relying on such agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of commercial success/profitability only as tied to patented features
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success, established profitability, or popularity of an accused product is relevant only insofar as the success is attributable to the patented features rather than non-patented features or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury instructions should caution jurors that product-level success must be apportioned to the patented contribution; otherwise Factor 8 (commercial success) can improperly inflate royalty awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of duration and term of license
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration of the patent and the term of any license are relevant ex ante factors in determining appropriate royalty amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor 7 (duration/term) is relevant to what the parties would have negotiated ex ante; instructions should explain how term affects bargaining and present the parties' contentions regarding term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of commercial relationship and competitive context
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial relationships between licensor and licensee (competitors vs. non-competitors, inventor/promoter relationships, etc.) affect bargaining positions and thus are relevant to the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor 5 guidance: courts should instruct juries to consider such relationships only insofar as they reflect ex ante expectations and bargaining dynamics at the negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction on manner of performing the damages calculation and tying to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury should be instructed on the step-by-step manner of performing the damages calculation and how the damages determination relates to the particular facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions should provide structure (identify base, apportion, select royalty form and rate, compute total). They should direct jurors to use case-specific evidence and to avoid generic or untethered numeric recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-verdict reasonable royalties (consideration for post-verdict damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries (or courts) should be instructed about how a reasonable royalty determination applies post-verdict, if applicable (i.e., whether and how a royalty would operate after judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the parties dispute post-verdict royalties, the instruction should explain available forms (running vs. lump-sum) and how to calculate them consistent with ex ante principles and apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportion to exclude value from other patents, manufacturing, risks, or infringer improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly instruct jurors to exclude portions of value attributable to other patents, the manufacturing process, business risks, or improvements added by the infringer when determining the portion of realizable profit credited to the invention (Georgia-Pacific Factor 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that failure to apportion leads to systemic overcompensation. Provide examples and require evidentiary support for any allocation of value to the patented feature.
